The cost of hitting a given performance target varies by more than an order of magnitude across the model market. Reaching a **40% solve rate on Terminal-Bench** can cost anywhere from **under $1 to over $60**; reaching **70%** runs from roughly **$10 to over $180**. And the cheapest model is not the same one at both targets — relative cost-effectiveness shifts with the difficulty of the bar.

That dispersion is the raw material for **computational arbitrage**: an intermediary buys inference from a portfolio of models, allocates a budget across them, and resells the result at a profit.

## The Hardness Result

A paper from the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and the Tübingen AI Center (Okati, Olmedo, Hardt — Olmedo being the author of the original computational-arbitrage framing) formalizes arbitrage as a **budget-allocation problem**: maximize expected utility, which is the probability that at least one model in the portfolio solves the query, subject to a total spend.

**Theorem 1: finding the optimal arbitrage policy is NP-hard.** With an unbounded model market, exhaustive allocation search is computationally infeasible.

The escape hatch is a condition on how performance scales with inference spending: whenever spending has **diminishing returns in log-failure reduction**, the objective becomes jointly concave and the global optimum is computable efficiently even in large markets. The paper also develops a **sample-efficient empirical-Bayes estimator** for recovering query-level utility curves from limited data — the practical bottleneck, since measuring true utility normally means paying for many model calls.

## What It Predicts About Markets

Three economic consequences fall out of the optimum:

- every funded model delivers the **same marginal utility per dollar** — revenue flows to providers whose performance justifies their price
- arbitrage directs revenue **away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices**
- arbitrage **rewards complementary specialization**, so providers compete either by being cheap generalists or by being specialists on queries others fail

Experiments across **LiveCodeBench, Terminal-Bench 2.0, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and DeepSWE** show the portfolio consistently improves the cost-performance frontier over any individual model, with the largest gains at intermediate budgets. A greedy deployment order (highest expected utility per cost on queries missed by earlier models) tracks the best order found by exhaustive search, unlike the cheapest-first heuristic.

The honest caveat: this is a theory paper with modest-scale experiments, and real marketplaces have contract, latency, and data-handling constraints that the allocation model abstracts away entirely. But the direction of travel is clear — inference brokers are the next layer between model providers and enterprise buyers, and the pricing rules governing that layer are being worked out now.

Paper: [arXiv:2610.40831](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40831) · [code](https://github.com/nastaran75/arbitrage-markets)
